column2: Then the Pandava, covering Drona's son with a thousand well-aimed arrows, let out a lion's roar.
Then Drona's son, warding off the arrows with arrows in the battle, struck the Pandava on the forehead with an iron arrow, as if smiling, O king.
The Pandava bore the arrow lodged in his forehead as a proud rhinoceros in the forest bears its horn, O king.
Then valiant Bhima pierced Drona's son, who was striving in battle, with three iron arrows in the forehead, as if in wonder.
With the arrows lodged in his forehead, that Brahmana shone like the best of mountains with three peaks drenched in the rains.
Drona's son maddened the Pandava with hundreds of arrows, but could not shake him, as the wind cannot shake a mountain.
Likewise the Pandava, delighted, could not shake Drona's son in battle with hundreds of sharp arrows, as a flood cannot shake a mountain.
Those two great chariot-warriors, covering each other with dreadful arrows, skilled in chariot-play, shone, heroes fierce in battle.
Blazing like two suns that destroy the worlds, they scorched each other with the best of arrows as if with their own rays.
Striving to repay each other in the great battle, they exerted themselves fearlessly in return for each blow.
Those two great chariot-warriors ranged in battle like two tigers, with arrows for fangs, hard to withstand, with bows gaping, terrible.
They became invisible on all sides behind nets of arrows, like the moon and sun covered by masses of cloud in the sky.
And in a moment those two tamers of foes became visible again, like the moon and sun freed from the cloud in the sky.
Then Drona's son circled Vrikodara to the left, showering him with hundreds of fierce arrows like streams of rain on a mountain.
Bhima could not bear that mark of his enemy's victory and, O king, circled him in turn to the left.
In their circlings and divisions, advancing and retreating, a tumultuous fight took place between them in that great battle.
Having traversed various paths, circles and stations, they struck each other with arrows drawn full length and loosed.
Those two great chariot-warriors strove to kill each other, and tried to leave each other without a chariot in the fight.
Then the great chariot-warrior, Drona's son, brought forth great weapons, and the Pandava countered them in battle with weapons.
Then, O great king, a terrible weapon-duel took place, like the dreadful conflict of planets at the destruction of creatures.
The arrows loosed by those two clashed, O Bharata, lighting up all quarters and the army on all sides.
The terrible sky was covered with masses of arrows, as if with falling meteors at the destruction of creatures, O king.
From the collision of arrows, O Bharata, a fire arose with sparks and blazing flames, and it burnt both armies.
Siddhas there, O great king, flying past, said: "All other battles are surpassed; this battle is greater still.
All other battles do not equal a sixteenth part of this; such a battle never was, nor will be again.
Ah, both are endowed with knowledge and fierce prowess! Ah, the terrible strength in Bhima, and these two's skill in weapons!
Ah, the essence of their valour, ah, their dexterity! These two stand in battle like Time, Death and Yama.
Like two Rudras come into being, like two suns, or like two Yamas are these two tigers among men in dreadful form in battle."

At that time the voices of the siddhas were heard again and again, and a lion-roar arose from the assembled dwellers in heaven on seeing the marvellous and inconceivable deed of those two in the battle.
Those two heroes in battle, O king, each having wronged the other, looked at each other in anger with rolling eyes.
Their eyes red with rage, their lips trembling with rage, biting their teeth and lips in rage,
the two great chariot-warriors covered each other with showers of arrows, with streams of arrows for water and weapons for lightning in battle.
Piercing each other's banners and charioteers, those two great chariot-warriors pierced each other's horses and wounded each other.
Then, O great king, enraged, both took arrows in the great fight and swiftly hurled them at each other, desiring each other's death.
Those two arrows, O great king, shining at the front of the army, met and struck each other, thunderbolt-swift and irresistible.
Struck hard by each other's impetus and by the arrows, those two great heroes fell on the seats of their own chariots.
Then the charioteer, knowing Drona's son to be unconscious, carried him away from the battle, O king, in the sight of all kshatriyas.
Likewise the charioteer carried the Pandava, scorcher of foes, who was faint again and again, away from the fight in his chariot.
[Sanjaya said:] Hear, O king, as I tell the battle as it happened, the combat of heroes with their enemies that destroys the sins of the body.
Partha, entering the Samshaptaka host like an ocean, agitated it, slayer of foes, as a great wind agitates the sea.
Dhananjaya, crushing the heads of heroes with sharp broad-headed arrows—faces bright as the full moon, with fine eyes, brows and teeth—quickly strewed the earth as with lotuses cut from their stalks.
Arjuna in the battle cut off with razor-arrows the well-rounded, long, stout arms of the foe, adorned with sandal and aguru, bearing weapons and armour, like five-headed serpents.
Pandava again and again cut with broad-headed arrows the yoke-bearers, the better yoke-bearers, the charioteers, banners, bows, arrows, hands and elbows.
In the battle Arjuna, O king, sent elephants, horses, chariots and their riders to Yama's abode with many thousands of arrows.
Roaring like bulls, they rushed up against that hero, enraged, with shouts of "Hum", and struck him as he struck them, with arrows, as bulls with horns.
Their fight with him became hair-raising, like that of the daityas with the thunderbolt-wielder for the conquest of the three worlds.
Arjuna smashed chariots whose triple poles, wheels and axles were cut, whose warriors, horses and charioteers were slain, whose weapons and quivers were shattered, and whose banners were torn down,
whose reins and traces were severed, whose three-fold poles and yokes were destroyed, whose supports and yokes were broken, and whose weapon rows were scattered, as the wind scatters great clouds.
Astonishing, a sight to behold, increasing his foes' fear, Arjuna did the work of a thousand great chariot-warriors.
Hosts of siddhas, gods and sages, and charanas praised him; celestial drums sounded and showers of flowers fell on the heads of Keshava and Arjuna, and a bodiless voice spoke.

The splendour, light, strength and radiance of the moon, sun, wind and fire which those two heroes always bear—these are Keshava and Arjuna.
mahabharata:8:12.16	Unconquerable like Brahma and Ishana, heroes standing on a single chariot, best of all beings, the heroes are Nara and Narayana both.
Having seen and heard this great marvel, O Bharata, Ashvatthaman, well prepared, rushed at the two Krishnas in the battle.
Then, calling to the Pandava who was shooting arrows like Yama and Time the Ender, with his bow in hand, Drona's son said, laughing:
If you, hero, regard me as a worthy guest who has arrived, then with all your heart today give me the hospitality of battle.
Thus challenged by the preceptor's son, eager to fight, Arjuna thought highly of himself and said this to Janardana:
The Samshaptakas are to be slain by me, and Drona's son challenges me; whatever is to be done next, command me, O mighty-armed one.
Thus addressed, Krishna carried Partha to the side of Drona's son, as the wind brings Indra at a sacrifice when called with the rite of victory.
Greeting him, with single mind Keshava said to Drona's son: "Ashvatthaman, be steady, strike quickly and endure.
This is the time for those who live on a master's food to repay it. The disputes of Brahmanas are subtle; the victory and defeat of kshatriyas are gross.
The divine honour of Partha that you cannot tolerate through delusion—wishing to obtain it, fight steadily today against the Pandava."
Thus told by Vasudeva, the best of the twice-born said "So be it", and pierced Keshava with sixty iron arrows and Arjuna with three.
Arjuna, greatly enraged, cut his bow with three broad-headed arrows; then Drona's son took up another, more terrible bow.
Stringing it in an instant, he pierced Arjuna and Keshava with three arrows—Vasudeva with three and the Pandava with a thousand.
Then Drona's son, exerting himself, let loose thousands, tens of thousands and hundreds of millions of arrows, checking Arjuna in the battle.
From his quiver, bow, bowstring, fingers, O revered one, from his arms, hands, chest, mouth, nose and eyes,
from his ears, head and limbs, from the roots of his hairs, and from his chariot and banners, arrows issued, as if by the speakers of the Veda.
Piercing Keshava and the Pandava with a great net of arrows, Drona's son, delighted, roared with the sound of a mass of great clouds.
Hearing him roar, the Pandava said to Achyuta: "See, Madhava, the wickedness of Drona's son towards me.
Having brought us into his house of arrows, he thinks us fit to be killed. I shall destroy this design of his by skill and by strength."
Cutting Ashvatthaman's hurled arrows one by one into three pieces each, the best of the Bharatas dispersed them as wind disperses mist.
Then the Pandava again pierced the Samshaptakas, with their horses, charioteers, chariots and elephants, and masses of banners and infantry, with fierce arrows.
Whoever and whatever form they saw there, in whatever manner, each thought himself and that thing pierced by arrows.
Driven by Gandiva, those winged arrows of many shapes killed, standing at a distance of a krosha and more, elephants and men in battle.
Severed trunks of rutting elephants fell, cut by broad-headed arrows, like autumn trees in full growth cut by axes.
Afterwards those elephants with their riders fell like mountains, like masses of hills shattered by the thunderbolt-wielder's bolt.
Chariots like gandharva cities, duly equipped, with trained steeds, occupied by warriors arrogant in battle,
he shattered with arrows, raining on his foes; Dhananjaya struck horse-riders, adorned ones, and footmen.
Dhananjaya, like the sun at the end of an age, dried up the great ocean of the Samshaptakas, hard to dry, with the sharp rays of his arrows.
Again he swiftly pierced the great mountain that was Drona's son with iron arrows like the sun, of great speed, as the thunderbolt-wielder a mountain.
Enraged, the preceptor's son, eager to fight, could not fight that Partha, who cut his swift arrows aimed at his horses and charioteer midway.
Then, extremely enraged, he loosed quivers of arrows, as a host would give houses to a guest suited to Ashvatthaman.
Then the Pandava, leaving the Samshaptakas, went to Drona's son, as a giver leaves one unfit for the row and turns to a suppliant who is fit.
Then a battle took place between those two, of the radiance of Shukra and Angiras (Brihaspati), like Shukra and Angiras in the sky around a star.
Tormenting each other with the blazing rays of arrows, they became terrifiers of the world, like two planets out of their course.
Then Arjuna pierced him hard between the eyebrows with an iron arrow; with it Drona's son shone like the sun with upward rays.
Then the two Krishnas, greatly tormented by hundreds of Ashvatthaman's arrows, shone like the suns of the end of an age with masses of rays and nets.
Then Arjuna, guarded by Vasudeva, loosed a weapon streaming on every side and struck Drona's son with arrows like the thunderbolt, fire and Vaivasvata's rod.
That exceedingly splendid one of terrible deeds pierced Keshava and Arjuna in their vitals with well-loosed arrows of exceeding speed, by which even Death, if struck, would suffer.
Arjuna, warding off Drona's son's arrows with twice as many feather-shafted arrows, covered him, the lone hero, with his horses, charioteer and banner, and attacked the Samshaptaka army.
Bows, arrows, quivers, bowstrings, hands, arms, weapons held in hand, parasols, standards, horses, garments, garlands and ornaments,
shields, armour, desires, all their dear ones and heads of the foes standing facing him, Partha cut with his loosed arrows.
Well-arrayed chariots, horses and elephants, manned by heroes who had made their effort, were cast down by Partha's volleys of arrows and fell with those best of men.
Heads of men, with faces like lotus, sun and full moon, crowned with diadems and garlands, cut by broad-headed, half-moon and razor arrows, fell constantly on the earth.
Then Kalinga, Vanga, Anga and Nishada heroes, on elephants like those of the lord of the gods, filled with the pride and fury of the gods' enemies, rushed at the Pandava eager to kill him.
Partha cut the armour, vital parts, trunks and drivers of those elephants, and then standards and banners fell, like peaks of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
When they were crushed, Kiritin covered the preceptor's son with arrows of the colour of the new sun, with great nets of cloud, as wind covers the sun in its rising.
Then Drona's son, hurling aside Arjuna's arrows with arrows, covered Arjuna and Vasudeva with arrows like the moon and sun in the sky, and roared like a cloud at the end of summer.
Arjuna, tormented by him and those of your side whose weapons were uncut, suddenly made a darkness of arrows and pierced them all with feather-shafted arrows.
He was not seen taking, aiming or loosing arrows in the battle, Savyasachin; only slain elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and chariots with bodies pierced through were seen.
Aiming ten excellent iron arrows, Drona's son quickly loosed them, as it were, as one; five of them pierced Arjuna and five well-loosed ones pierced Achyuta.
Struck by them, those two best of men, streaming blood, resembling Kubera and Indra, seemed overcome as by one of exhausted knowledge; what did others think—that they were slain?
Then the lord of the Dasharhas said to Arjuna: "Why are you careless? Kill this warrior! If neglected he would do harm, like an untreated disease that becomes troublesome."
Saying "So be it" to Achyuta, the vigilant one with effort shot Drona's son with arrows, cut his horses' reins and pierced the horses; they carried him far away from the battle.
Turning back, the wise one, best of the Angirases, reflecting, knew that victory was sure for the Vrishni hero and Dhananjaya, and did not wish to renew the fight with Partha.
With Ashvatthaman carried off by his horses from the battle, with his body reversed, like a disease removed from the body by charms, herbs, rites and gifts,
Keshava and Arjuna advanced towards the Samshaptakas in a chariot, its banner fluttering in the wind, with a sound like a flood.
Turning the chariot, Keshava, urging the horses swift as Garuda and wind, said to Arjuna:

The Magadha king has also advanced on a crushing elephant, not inferior to Bhagadatta in skill and strength.
mahabharata:8:13.4	Having killed him you shall again kill the Samshaptakas. At the end of this speech he brought Partha near Dandadhara.
That foremost of the Magadhas, a master of the goad, irresistible among planets, a fearsome planet-like figure, crushed the enemy's army, as a comet, a fierce planet, crushes the whole earth.
Mounted on a well-equipped elephant like a danava, thundering like a great cloud, crusher of foes, he killed by thousands hosts of chariots, horses and elephants with arrows and even elephants.
Standing on his chariot, he swiftly smote horses, charioteers and chariots; on foot he struck elephants with feet and trunk; mounted on an elephant he slew like a wheel of Time.
Felling men adorned with black-iron armour with their horses and footmen, he smote them with the best of elephants, mighty, as one crushes thick reeds with a noise.

Then Arjuna, amid the sound of bowstrings and wheel-rims, mridangas, kettledrums and many conches, and the cries of thousands of men, horses and elephants, rushed with his excellent chariot at that excellent elephant.
Then Dandadhara, wishing to disturb Janardana and Dhananjaya greatly, struck Arjuna with javelins from an elephant with broken temples, dark as a cloud, with the speed of wind.
Then with three razor-arrows the Pandava cut off both his arms, like elephant trunks, and his head, whose face was like the full moon, at once; then he tormented the elephant with hundreds of arrows.
That elephant, in golden armour, pierced by Partha's arrows adorned with gold, shone like a mountain at night with herbs and trees ablaze with a forest fire.
Pained, roaring like a cloud, reeling, wheeling, stumbling, distressed and fleeing, it fell wounded with its driver, like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt.
When his brother was slain in battle with the snow-white elephant with golden garlands, like a peak of the Himalaya, Danda came on, wishing to kill Dhananjaya, younger brother of Indra.
He pierced Janardana with three javelins bright as sunbeams and Arjuna with five, and roared; then the Pandava cut off his arms.
Cut off by razor-arrows, his two arms, with javelins, armlets fallen, smeared with sandal, falling from the elephant together, shone like two great serpents falling from a mountain peak.
Then the head of Danda, cut off with a half-moon arrow by Kiritin, fell from the elephant to the ground; blood-red as it fell, it shone like the sun setting in the western quarter.
Then Partha pierced the elephant, like a white mountain peak, with the best of arrows like the rays of the sun; it fell roaring, like a peak of the Himalaya struck by a thunderbolt.
Then other best elephants like it, eager to conquer Savyasachin in battle, were made by him exactly as those two elephants had been; thus the great army of the enemy broke.
Elephants, chariots, horses and men in hosts, killing each other, fell in the battle, stumbling over one another and struck down, and those bearing the speech of their various clans were slain.
Then his own soldiers surrounded Arjuna and said, as gods to Purandara: "We have been delivered from fear, as creatures from death. Hero, by good fortune the enemy has been slain by you.
If you had not protected these people, afflicted by fear of mighty foes, it would have been a joy to the enemy; as it is, with these enemies slain by you here, we are glad."
Hearing such words repeatedly from his friends, Arjuna, glad, honoured those people as was fitting and went again to slay the Samshaptaka hosts.
Struck by Partha's arrows, men, horses, chariots and elephants, O king, wandered, reeled, shrieked, fell and fainted, O revered one.
Cutting the yoke-bearers, the better yoke-bearers, the charioteers, the chariots, hands, weapons in hand, arms and heads,
the Pandava cut down with broad-headed arrows, razor-arrows, half-moons and calf-tooth arrows the enemy heroes fighting back in battle.
Eager to fight, hundreds and thousands of heroes rushed at Arjuna like bulls at a bull over a cow.
Their battle with him was hair-raising, like that of the daityas with the thunderbolt-wielder for the conquest of the three worlds.
He pierced him with three arrows like fangs of serpents; then Ugrayudha cut his head from his body.
Enraged on all sides, they rained weapons of many kinds on Arjuna, like clouds driven by the Maruts upon the Himalaya in the hot season.
Arjuna, warding off the enemies' weapons with weapons on all sides, slew many of them together with well-loosed arrows.
Their costly chariots, shattered there, appeared in many places like the houses of rich men destroyed by fire, wind and water.
Elephants with vital parts pierced by arrows like thunderbolts fell like mountain-peak houses struck by thunder, wind and fire.
Many horses with riders fell, struck by Arjuna, with tongues and entrails out, wasted on the ground, blood-soaked and hard to look at.
Men, horses and elephants pierced through by iron arrows from Savyasachin reeled, stumbled, fell, roared and fainted, O revered one.
With stone-whetted and dreadful arrows like thunderbolt and poison, Partha slew them as Mahendra slew the danavas.
Heroes with costly armour and ornaments, with weapons and garments of many forms, with chariots and banners, slain by Partha, lay still.
Conquered, they of meritorious deeds and distinguished lineage and fame went, with their bodies on earth, to heaven by their mighty deeds.
Then your heroes, lords of various countries, with their troops, rose in anger and rushed at Arjuna's chariot.
Borne by chariots and horses, and foot-soldiers eager to kill, they rushed on, quickly hurling weapons of every kind.
That great shower of weapons hurled by the warriors like great clouds, Arjuna, like the wind, quickly dispelled with sharp arrows.
Wishing to cross suddenly that great flood of weapons, with its horses, foot-soldiers, elephants and chariots, Partha did so by a bridge of weapons.
Then Vasudeva said to Partha: "Why do you play, sinless one? Having crushed these Samshaptakas, hasten to the slaying of Karna."
Saying "So be it", Arjuna quickly dispersed the remaining Samshaptakas with weapons by force, as Indra slew the daityas.
In the battle Arjuna was not seen by any taking or aiming arrows, nor was he seen by any quickly loosing them.
Saying "A marvel!", Govinda urged the horses; the swans (white horses) entered the army as swans enter a lake.
Then, as the slaughter of men proceeded on that battlefield, Govinda, looking on it, spoke to Savyasachin:

Partha, this terrible destruction of the Bharatas is going on, a great one of the kings of the earth, for Duryodhana's sake.
mahabharata:8:14.28	Behold, Bharata, the golden-backed bows of great archers cast away, and the quivers and arrow-cases,
mahabharata:8:14.29	golden-feathered arrows with bent joints, iron arrows washed in oil, loosed like serpents,
mahabharata:8:14.30	swords with ivory hilts adorned with gold, javelins and bows scattered, variegated and gold-adorned,
mahabharata:8:14.31	armour cast away with golden backs, O Bharata, lances of gold, darts adorned with gold,
mahabharata:8:14.32	large maces bound with bands of gold, spears of gold, pattishas adorned with gold,
mahabharata:8:14.33	axes thrown down with golden-painted handles, pestles with iron goads fallen, and heavy clubs,
mahabharata:8:14.34	look at the variegated shataghnis, broad iron bars, discs thrown away and many hammers in the battle.
mahabharata:8:14.35	Holding weapons of many kinds, eager for victory, the mighty ones, bereft of life, appear as if alive.
mahabharata:8:14.36	See thousands of warriors with limbs crushed by maces, heads split by pestles, and ground by elephants, horses and chariots.
mahabharata:8:14.37	The battlefields, slayer of foes, are covered with the lifeless bodies of men, elephants and horses, torn by arrows, darts, spears, javelins, swords, pattishas, lances, claws and clubs,
mahabharata:8:14.38	bodies variously rent and drenched in floods of blood.
mahabharata:8:14.39	The earth, O Bharata, shines with arms smeared with sandal, with armlets, fine ornaments, with arm-guards and bracelets,
mahabharata:8:14.40	adorned with severed forearms and hands thrown about, and with the severed thighs of the mighty, like elephants' trunks,
mahabharata:8:14.41	with the heads of bull-eyed heroes, with their topknots tied and with fine jewels and earrings cut off, the earth shines.
mahabharata:8:14.42	With headless trunks smeared with blood, with limbs and heads severed, the earth shines, best of the Bharatas, like fires whose flames have died.
mahabharata:8:14.43	See the many shattered chariots with golden bells, fine and shattered, and the horses, many of them, drenched in blood.
Lamenting again and again "Alas, Karna! Alas, Karna!", with difficulty he went to his own camp with the kings who survived.
In fear of pursuit, turning away, they fled again; after going a short while, their horses weary and themselves thirsty,
Sanjaya, of great wisdom, approached him who had fallen dumb in thought, overwhelmed with anxiety, and spoke.
Other twice-born, learned in the Veda and of trained intellect, householders and snatakas, all saw the best of the Kurus.
What could be more painful than that, for my sake, the grandsire was brought to this state in the field of battle by his enemies, and likewise other kings with their sons and kinsmen?
Seeing the lord of men dejected and bereft of spirit, the Pandavas, again overcome by grief, sat down.
Vidura and Sanjaya attended on Dhritarashtra, and so did the wise Yuyutsu, the Kaurava, son of the vaishya woman.
After some time the Kuru king Yudhishthira heard that the Vrishni circle had been slain in the pestle affair.
Knowing Arjuna's opinion, Bhimasena and the twins accepted the words spoken by Savyasachin.
Radiant like the sun and surrounded by heroic glory, he saw him seated with the shining gods and the Sadhyas of meritorious deeds.
